name: Battle of Alesia
info: Julius Caesar's Roman army besieged the Gallic leader Vercingetorix and his allies in the fortified settlement of Alesia in September 52 BCE, beat off a Gallic relief force, and ended organised Gallic resistance.

facts.place: Around the Gallic oppidum of Alesia, a centre of the Mandubii, most probably on Mont Auxois above Alise-Sainte-Reine in the Côte-d'Or, France
facts.sides: Rome under the proconsul Julius Caesar, against a confederation of Gallic tribes under Vercingetorix of the Arverni; about 80,000 men are said to have been in Alesia, and the relief force is put at a quarter of a million by Caesar and at 50,000 to 100,000 by modern historians
facts.outcome: The relief force was beaten off and fled, Vercingetorix surrendered, and the Gallic revolt collapsed

t: The Romans built two lines of fortifications round Alesia, an inner one against the besieged Gauls and an outer one against the relief force, and the Gauls' combined attacks on them failed.
Caesar's figure of a quarter of a million for the relief force is probably an exaggeration; modern historians usually think a number between 50,000 and 100,000 more credible.
Alesia was the last major engagement between Gauls and Romans and the end of generalised, organised resistance, although Gaul did not become a Roman province until 27 BCE.
dyk: Excavations at Alise-Sainte-Reine in the 1860s, funded by Napoleon III, uncovered evidence of Roman camps, and a statue of Vercingetorix was then dedicated at the site.
ev: Caesar becomes proconsul of Cisalpine Gaul, Illyricum and Gallia Narbonensis and begins the Gallic Wars
Caesar announces that Gaul is to be treated as a Roman province
Vercingetorix unites a coalition of Gauls and revolts, and the Romans take Avaricum
Caesar is defeated at Gergovia and then beats Vercingetorix's cavalry at the Vingeanne
Caesar besieges Alesia, fends off the relief force and receives Vercingetorix's surrender
Caesar crosses the Rubicon, beginning the Roman Civil War
Vercingetorix is paraded in Caesar's triumph and garrotted
Gallic territories north of Gallia Narbonensis become a Roman province under Augustus

sections.background:
In 58 BCE, after his first consulship in 59 BCE, Julius Caesar was appointed proconsul of Cisalpine Gaul, Illyricum and Gallia Narbonensis. A proconsular term was meant to last one year, but his was set at an unprecedented five, and he commanded four legions. In the Gallic Wars (58–50 BCE) he defeated the Helvetii and the Suebi, crossed the Rhine in 55 BCE, intervened in disputes among the Gauls in 57 BCE and marched on the Belgae. From then on he conquered the Gallic peoples one by one. His successes brought him political prestige in Rome and great wealth through the spoils of war and the sale of war captives as slaves.

The campaigns of 53 BCE were harsh, and the Gauls feared for their prosperity. In that year Caesar announced that Gaul was to be treated as a Roman province, subject to Roman laws and religion. The Gauls feared that the Romans would destroy their holy land, watched over by the Carnutes, where the druids met each year to mediate between the tribes. The threat to their sacred lands united peoples who had not been united before. Over the winter Vercingetorix, the king of the Arverni, assembled an unprecedented coalition of Gauls.
sections.forces:
The Roman commanders named in the fighting are Caesar, Marc Antony, Caius Trebonius, Labienus, Brutus and Caius Fabius, and Caesar also had Germanic allies, who pursued the Gallic cavalry. The Gauls were led by Vercingetorix of the Arverni, who had avoided open battle that year, raided foraging parties and supply trains, and abandoned oppida he could not hold. After defeat at the Vingeanne he withdrew to Alesia, an oppidum on a lofty hill with two rivers on two sides, where about 80,000 men are said to have been garrisoned beside the local civilians. He intended Alesia as a trap for a pincer attack on the Romans and sent for a relief army at once.

Caesar chose to starve the place out. His contravallation round Alesia was eleven Roman miles (16 km) long with 23 redoubts, and his outer circumvallation, facing the other way, ran for 14 Roman miles (20.7 km). Caesar describes trenches, one filled with river water, a palisaded rampart, turrets every 80 pedes, and hidden pits with stakes and hooked stakes before the lines. Archaeology suggests the lines were not continuous, as he claims, and made much use of the terrain. For the relief force Caesar gives a quarter of a million, probably an exaggeration; modern historians usually think a number between 50,000 and 100,000 more credible.
sections.course:
The Gauls sallied on horseback while the works were going up, and before they were finished Vercingetorix sent out all his cavalry by night to rally the tribes. When the relief force arrived it camped on a hill a mile from the Roman lines, and the next day attacked the outer fortification while the besieged Gauls attacked the inner one. The combined attack failed. The Gauls attacked again by night; Marc Antony and Caius Trebonius brought troops from the remotest forts, and at first light the relief force withdrew for fear of being surrounded. Vercingetorix's men were delayed by having to fill trenches and returned to the town.

The Gauls then noticed that the north side of a hill could not be included in the Roman works, and a camp of two legions stood there on steep, disadvantageous ground. They chose 60,000 men under Vercassivellaunus, a near relative of Vercingetorix, who marched before dawn and attacked at noon, while Vercingetorix sallied against any weak part of the inner line. Caesar sent Labienus, Brutus and Caius Fabius with cohorts, then came himself with fresh troops. Labienus was close to collapse when Caesar arrived. The Roman cavalry appeared behind the Gauls, who fled and were intercepted and slaughtered. Caesar wrote that the whole enemy force could have been destroyed had the soldiers not been wearied.
sections.aftermath:
After the repeated failures the relieving army melted away. The next day Vercingetorix called the Gallic council and proposed that he be killed or surrendered alive to appease the Romans. Caesar ordered the Gauls to give up their weapons and deliver their chieftains, and Vercingetorix was surrendered. The captives were given to the Roman soldiers as spoils of war, apart from the Aedui and Arverni, whom Caesar hoped to win over. Earlier in the siege the people of Alesia had sent out their old, sick, wives and children to save food, hoping Caesar would take them in; he forbade it, and they were left between the lines to starve.

Caesar set his legions to winter in the lands of the defeated tribes. South-west Gaul was not yet pacified and there were mopping-up operations in 50 BCE. Vercingetorix was held in Rome for five years, paraded in Caesar's triumph and ritually garrotted in the Tullianum in 46 BCE. The Senate declared 20 days of thanksgiving but, for political reasons, refused Caesar a triumphal parade. Gaul was not formally made into provinces until the reign of Augustus in 27 BCE, and there may have been unrest as late as 70 CE.
sections.sources:
The event is described by Caesar himself in his Commentarii de Bello Gallico, and by later ancient authors, namely Plutarch and Cassius Dio. After 50 BCE Aulus Hirtius took over the writing of Caesar's reports on the war. The only records are Roman and so presumed to be biased, and figures for armies and casualties have always been a propaganda weapon and are suspect. Caesar's quarter of a million for the relief force is probably an exaggeration meant to enhance his victory. His reports elsewhere are doubted too: at Gergovia his casualty numbers are likely much lower than the real ones, and his claim to have sounded a retreat there is dubious.

Archaeology bears on the siege works. Modern excavation suggests Caesar's preparations were not as complete as he describes, though it is apparent that the works did their job. For many years the site was unknown. Alaise in the Franche-Comté and Alise-Sainte-Reine in the Côte-d'Or were the main candidates, and Napoleon III, who favoured the second, funded excavations in the 1860s that uncovered evidence of Roman camps. Research since then has established Alise-Sainte-Reine as most probably the site, and excavations in the 1990s led Colin Wells to say they should have removed all doubt. Other proposals, such as Chaux-des-Crotenay, are not accepted by the vast majority of the scientific community.
sections.legacy:
Alesia is called the climactic engagement of the Gallic Wars, the last major engagement between Gauls and Romans, and a classic example of siege warfare and investment. It marked the end of Gallic independence in what is now France and Belgium. Paul K. Davis writes that Caesar's victory established Roman dominance in Gaul for the next 500 years and also created a rivalry with the Roman government. Adrian Goldsworthy writes that virtually all the tribes that rebelled capitulated and accepted the reality of conquest. Tom Holland writes that by the Romans' measure of a man's capacity to withstand ordeals of exhaustion and blood, Caesar had proved himself the foremost man in the Republic.

For Caesar the victory was a large personal success, militarily and politically. Political tension rose, and in 49 BCE he crossed the Rubicon, which precipitated the Roman Civil War of 49 to 45 BCE. He was made dictator for life in 44 BCE. His growing personal power and honours undermined the republican foundations of Rome, and civil wars followed his assassination, ending in Octavian's defeat of Marc Antony and the beginning of rule by emperors. Under Agrippa, the first governor of Gaul from 39–38 BCE, a radial road network was built centred on Lugdunum (Lyon). Napoleon III dedicated a statue of Vercingetorix at the site.

summary: In September 52 BCE Julius Caesar besieged Vercingetorix and his Gallic coalition in Alesia behind two lines of fortifications and beat off a large relief force. Vercingetorix surrendered, and organised Gallic resistance to Rome ended, though Gaul became a province only in 27 BCE.
references: Catherine Gilliver, Caesar's Gallic wars, 58–50 BC (Routledge, 2003)
notes: The article gives no Roman army strength and no casualty figures for Alesia; both are said plainly in the text. The only numbers are about 80,000 in Alesia, 60,000 chosen for the north-side attack, and the quarter of a million (Caesar) against 50,000 to 100,000 (modern historians usually) for the relief force. The article's 'Numbers involved' paragraph does not say outright that the 50,000-100,000 is the relief force alone; I read it so, since Caesar's figure it criticises is for the relief force.
The article's own lead says 'September 52 BC'; no day is given.
The 80,000 in Alesia: 'about 80,000 men were garrisoned in Alesia, together with the local civilian population'; I wrote 'said to have been' and 'beside the local civilians'.

Self-contradiction: the article says the relief force 'encamped on a hill one mile from the Roman fortification', and elsewhere that the outer line was built against it; the article says 'Marc Antony and Caius Trebonius' and cohorts 'of cavalry' for Labienus and others (I wrote 'cohorts').
Mismatch: the article says the Arverni kept their independence 'thanks to their victory at Gergovia' yet also says Arverni captives were spared at Alesia; I left the independence claim out.
The article says Vercingetorix 'left his people out between the fortifications to starve to death'; I wrote that they were left between the lines to starve.

Left out: Avaricum's 40,000 slain (Caesar's claim) and the rape and looting there, Gergovia's 700 dead including 46 centurions, the full fortification measurements, and the site-theory aside on Colin Wells's 'passionate nonsense'.
The Germanic allies pursuing the Gallic cavalry and the opening cavalry sallies are the article's account of the building phase, before the relief force came.
